Strait of Hormuz over the last 48 hours: tanker attacks continue

Iran's demands for opening the Strait of Hormuz are a nonstarter for the US. As I covered over the weekend, Iran has now added Palestine, Yemen, and Iraq along with Lebanon for a complete ceasefire as a condition. In addition, it also wants compensation for the war damages and the MOU violation. 

On the shipping front, Oman lane transits continue, but here's the catch. ADNOC (UAE) ships are being attacked with 4 of them getting hit last week and another possible attack today. ADNOC's rescue boat was sent out, but no other confirmation on the attack has been announced so far.

What is interesting is this. Iraqi crude is getting through the Oman lane. Prosperity tankers carrying Iraqi crude have not been hit.

Why?

Simple. In the past, Iran has exported some of its oil through Iraq to evade sanctions. This is one of the main reasons why we are not seeing all the tankers get hit through the Oman lane.

But it seems clear from the recent escalation patterns that whatever secret deal Iran had with UAE is all but over.

President Trump told reporters Monday that the U.S. controlled the Strait of Hormuz but admitted that Iran "can make trouble" in the key waterway.

"We control the strait 100%," Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office after signing an executive order on childhood vaccine recommendations. "Now, can they make trouble? Yeah, they can make trouble, but they're broke, they have no money."

Mr. Trump called the U.S. Navy's blockade on Iranian-bound ships a "steel wall" and "infallible," and he described the situation in the strait with Iran as "a little bit complex."

"They will, on occasion, drop a mine, and we find the mines," the president said. https://t.co/wVgpvclLno

#Agriculture: Global food prices rose to a three-year high last month as summer heatwaves and conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East lifted crop costs, potentially feeding through to higher consumer prices in the coming months. The UN FAO Food Price Index reached its highest since January 2023, although the year-on-year increase remained contained at just 1%. Sugar led the monthly rise at 5.6%, followed by grains at 3.4% and vegetable oils at 2%, while meat fell 2.8% and dairy declined 0.7%.
